paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised quantum machine learning for fraud detection

summary: This paper studies gate-based quantum kernel methods for credit-card fraud detection on a reduced Kaggle dataset of 500 samples with 25 fraud cases, using up to 20 qubits/features and an IQP-style feature map with data re-uploading depth d=3. The key quantitative result is that the quantum kernel methods outperform classical RBF baselines by about 15% average precision in the unsupervised OC-SVM setting at 20 qubits, with the classical unsupervised benchmark saturating around AP ≈ 0.55 and the quantum model reaching about 0.7.

experiments.description: Unsupervised fraud detection using quantum kernel-based one-class SVM with an IQP feature map and data re-uploading, evaluated on a credit card fraud dataset across 1 to 20 qubits/features and compared against classical RBF-kernel OC-SVM.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel OC-SVM with IQP feature map and data re-uploading (d=3)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: No trainable quantum parameters; fixed feature map. Classical OC-SVM hyperparameters tuned by random search over C and gamma.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; features are scaled and embedded via data-dependent rotations and pairwise ZZ interactions in an IQP-like circuit. The kernel is computed from the return probability after applying U_phi(x) and the inverse circuit for x'.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Unsupervised anomaly detection via one-class SVM: separate nominal transactions from anomalies using a kernel-induced decision boundary; maximize average precision on fraud class for evaluation.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: OC-SVM novelty detection with nu controlling the estimated anomaly fraction; no explicit quantum constraints beyond kernel evaluation.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection on anonymized transaction data; unsupervised learning on nominal transactions with fraud as anomalies.

dataset_specification.description: 28 anonymized features; time and amount features ignored; subsampled to 500 samples including 25 fraud examples; PCA applied to retain first N principal components; standard scaling before PCA; features scaled by eta=0.1 for quantum encoding

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Feature-wise standard scaling; PCA dimensionality reduction; subsampling to 500 samples with 25 fraud cases; quantum features additionally scaled by eta=0.1 to keep phases below 2π
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision (AP) used as threshold-free metric; results shown as a function of number of features/qubits; classical hyperparameters tuned by random search with cross-validation AP

hardware.classical_solver: scikit-learn OC-SVM and kernel evaluation on NVIDIA A100 GPU

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Standard scaling, PCA, subsampling, feature scaling by eta=0.1 for quantum encoding
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed from predicted anomaly scores; Gram matrices assembled from kernel evaluations

speedup_claims.conditions: unsupervised fraud detection at 20 qubits/features using IQP kernel with d=3 re-uploading
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported on a reduced dataset with 500 samples and 25 fraud cases; based on statevector simulation, not hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: O(N_s^2) training and O(N_d N_s) inference
speedup_claims.conditions: full Gram-matrix evaluation for quantum kernel training and inference
speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic quantum advantage proven; same quadratic scaling appears for classical kernel methods.

speedup_claims.factor: linear scaling with number of samples, O(N_s)
speedup_claims.conditions: if randomized protocols or adaptive detection are used for partial inference of Gram matrices
speedup_claims.caveats: Presented as a possible future improvement, not demonstrated in the experiment.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation requires O(N_s^2) Gram matrix construction for full training; inference O(N_d N_s) for Nd new samples
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical kernel methods also require O(N_s^2) Gram matrix construction
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: ~105 kernel evaluations for reduced dataset; ~O(N_s^2) for full Gram matrix

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Around 20 qubits/features for the reported separation; the paper also notes 50-100 qubits would be needed for strong separation.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Statevector simulation of IQP-style quantum kernels with up to 20 qubits; comparison against classical RBF OC-SVM on the same reduced fraud dataset.
limiting_factors: Need for many measurement shots on hardware
Potential insimulability on classical hardware is not resolved
Advantage is only a 15% AP gain at 20 qubits, not a demonstrated production advantage

notes: The paper explicitly states simulations with registers up to 20 qubits and use of PennyLane/JAX with statevector simulation on GPU.
Circuit depth is not given as a numeric depth; only the structure and re-uploading count d=3 are reported.
The paper explicitly reports unsupervised quantum kernels reaching about 0.7 AP at 20 qubits versus about 0.55 for classical RBF OC-SVM, i.e. roughly 15% higher AP.
This is a simulator result, not a hardware demonstration.

experiments.description: Supervised fraud classification using a quantum kernel feature map (IQP with data re-uploading) compared against classical logistic regression and classical SVC baselines across 1 to 20 qubits/features.

algorithm.variant: supervised quantum kernel classification with IQP feature map and data re-uploading (d=3)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: No trainable quantum parameters; fixed feature map.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; data embedded via x-dependent rotations and ZZ interactions in an IQP-like circuit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of fraud vs genuine transactions using a quantum kernel SVC-style decision function; evaluate average precision.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud classification on anonymized transaction data.

dataset_specification.description: 28 anonymized features; time and amount ignored; PCA preprocessing; standard scaling; feature scaling by eta=0.1 for quantum encoding

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Standard scaling, PCA dimensionality reduction, subsampling, and feature scaling by eta=0.1
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision versus number of features/qubits; compared to classical logistic regression and classical SVC with RBF kernels

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Standard scaling, PCA, subsampling, feature scaling by eta=0.1
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed for classification performance

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical logistic regression and classical SVC with RBF kernels
speedup_claims.conditions: supervised fraud classification beyond 10 qubits/features, with clear separation at 20 qubits
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide exact classical AP values in text; comparison is shown in Fig. 4(a).
No computational speedup is claimed; only predictive performance improvement is reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation requires O(N_s^2) Gram matrix construction
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical SVC kernel evaluation also requires O(N_s^2) Gram matrix construction

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Around 20 qubits/features for the reported separation; the paper also notes 50-100 qubits would be needed for strong separation.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Statevector simulation of IQP-style quantum kernels with up to 20 qubits; comparison against classical logistic regression and RBF SVC on the same reduced fraud dataset.
limiting_factors: No trainable quantum parameters, so advantage is from feature map expressivity only
The paper frames the result as promising but not yet industrially practical

notes: This is the supervised quantum-kernel classification experiment shown in Fig. 4(a).
The paper does not report a numeric circuit depth or shot count; only the re-uploading depth d=3 and up to 20 qubits are explicit.
The paper reports the quantum kernel classifier outperforming classical RBF-based supervised baselines by over ten percent AP at larger feature counts, with clear separation at 20 qubits.
This remains a simulation study rather than a QPU demonstration.

experiments.description: Classical supervised fraud classification benchmark using logistic regression and support vector classification (SVC) with RBF kernels, reported as the classical comparison for the quantum kernel classifier.

algorithm.optimizer: cross-validation/random search over C and gamma

key_results: Classical supervised benchmark shown in Fig. 2(a).
Average precision is lower than the quantum kernel model at larger feature counts; the paper states the quantum model reaches about 15% higher AP at 20 qubits/features.

experiments.description: Classical unsupervised fraud detection benchmark using one-class SVM with RBF kernels, compared against the quantum unsupervised kernel OC-SVM.

algorithm.optimizer: random search / cross-validation over C and gamma

key_results: Classical unsupervised benchmark shown in Fig. 2(b).
Average precision saturates around 0.55 at about 15 features.
